doc.title: Web Service APIs
doc.paragraph: There are two primary ways to interact with Adaptive Framework over the network. The traditional RESTful way allows you to send standard HTTP operations to the server and get status and results back with the appropriate content-type. This method is uri-based, like a typical RESTful service, and the HTTP operations map onto the adapter functions. Using the RESTful interface is particularly useful for web-based applications that are accustomed to RESTful ways to interact with object data.

section.title: REST
section.paragraph: The following table describes each HTTP request and the adapter function it calls:

row.column: POST, with an array of entries

section.paragraph: HTTP GET requests act as both get_object() and retrieve_objects() adapter session calls, depending on the HTTP URI that is specified. All HTTP URIs must specify an adapterId. When an Object Type and Object Id are also supplied, the GET is treated as a get_object(). When just the adapterId and Object Type are specified, the GET request is treated as a retrieve_objects() call.

A POST to an object's path changes that object in one of two ways, depending on the body. An array of entries, such as [["set_property", "title", "New"]], is a modify: each entry is applied in turn. An object is an update: each property in it replaces the one in the stored object, and the properties it leaves out stay as they are. A PUT replaces the whole object. Any other HTTP method, such as PATCH, fails with method_not_allowed.

For retrieve_objects() calls, you may also specify a query criteria, which is passed along to the retrieve_objects(). This is useful if you need to narrow down the results of the retrieve_objects(), or use an index to obtain performance. The query string is URL encoded RQL, for example GET /lmdb/Person/?sn=Hopper or GET /lmdb/Person/?and(eq(dept,ENG),ge(age,40)). See the Indexes chapter of the Administrative Guide for how queries use indexes.

A relation can be written as a function, ge(age,40), or with an operator between the property and the value, age=ge=40; dept=ENG is short for dept=eq=ENG. Lists go in parentheses and are separated by commas only, as in dept=in=(ENG,OPS) or n=out=(-1,2). A query string may also hold one sort() and one select(), joined to the filter with &:

Every value in a query string is text, and is compared as the data type the object type gives the property, so age=ge=40 compares numbers when age is declared an integer. A relation on a property an object does not have is false for that object. Characters the query string uses for itself must be percent encoded in a value, including +, which is written %2B: name=in=(a%2Bb,c) is the list a+b, c. A query string the server cannot read fails with syntax (HTTP 400), for example Expecting ',' or ')' in list.

For both GET requests, you may additionally specify object options to instruct the server on how to construct the object or objects that are being returned. For a complete list of options, see the Object Type description for _AdaptiveObjectOptions_.

The Content-Type header says how a request body is written, and the Accept header asks for the response in a content type. JSON (application/json) is always there and is the default. YAML (application/x-yaml) and UBJSON (application/ubjson) are there when the afw_yaml and afw_ubjson extensions are loaded, and application/x-afw is the framed form the JavaScript client, and so the admin app, uses for Perform Actions.

It's very easy to demonstrate how to use the RESTful API, using the command-line tool, curl. If you are running afwfcgi and have Apache or Nginx setup on the traditional Secure HTTP port 443, and you wanted to get the object afw of type _AdaptiveAdapter_, from the core adapter, afw, and you wanted it to be formatted with whitespace, you could run the following:
The _meta_ property holds the object's meta, such as its path and object type, next to its properties. Put the URL in quotes in a shell, since ; would otherwise end the command.

A journal adapter's entries are the object type _AdaptiveJournalEntry_. A GET of an entry's cursor returns that entry, and the journal functions are available as GETs of special object ids, each doing what the journal function of the same name does:
section.code: GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/get_first GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/get_by_cursor:<cursor> GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/get_next_after_cursor:<cursor> GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/get_next_for_consumer:<consumerId>[:<limit>] GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/get_next_for_consumer_after_cursor:<consumerId>:<cursor>[:<limit>] GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/advance_cursor_for_consumer:<consumerId>[:<limit>] GET /journal/_AdaptiveJournalEntry_/mark_consumed:<consumerId>:<cursor>
section.paragraph: A consumer form without a limit has no limit, and a limit must be 1 or more. The : does not need to be encoded. The Authorization chapter of the Administrative Guide describes how these requests are checked.
When a request fails, the response's HTTP status comes from the error's id, the same id a script sees as e.id in a catch. These are the ones a client meets most often:

row.column: A query string, object path or script that cannot be parsed
A query criteria object or modify body that is not valid
A script throw, or a function given the wrong arguments
A change to something that cannot be changed, such as an adapter that is read only
No such adapter, object type or object
An HTTP method the server does not handle, such as PATCH
The request went past a limit, such as limitRequestPoolBytes
A request Content-Type the server has no content type for
An operation the adapter does not have, such as a retrieve of journal entries

section.paragraph: A model's on* script can choose the status by giving its throw an id, such as throw "Person not found" id "not_found"; for a 404. The Throw statement in the Language Reference lists the ids a script may throw.

section.title: Perform Actions
section.paragraph: The second way to interact with Adaptive Framework remotely is to send HTTP POST payloads to the core adapter and specify which adaptive functions and parameters you'd like to interact with. This method requires clients to generate and receive payloads, but it offers some functionality that's not available through traditional REST. For example, you can call any adaptive function, not just the adapter ones. To use this technique, simply use HTTP POST actions to the Core adapter, afw, along with a payload to instruct the server which adaptive function to invoke and all of its parameters.
The body names each function and gives its parameters by name. One action can be sent on its own, or several in actions, which run in order:

The parameter names are the ones in each function's description in the Function Reference. An optional _flags_ array sets flags, such as response:metrics, while the actions run. The object type _AdaptiveActions_ describes the whole request.
The response has a status and, for each action, its result and the resultDataType of the result:
The actions stop at the first one that fails. The status is then error, and error holds the error object, with the actionNumber of the action that failed:
A single action's response has its result, resultDataType and status at the top.

section.title: Examples
section.paragraph: The following section provides some code samples for how to use a tool such as curl to interact with Adaptive Framework by creating, changing, and retrieving objects in different ways. Each write answers with a journal entry that shows the request and its status; an add's entry also has the new objectId and path.
section.code: curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json' \ -X POST http://localhost/vault/users/ \ -d @- <<EOF { "firstName": "John", "lastName": "Doe", "email": "john.doe@myorg.org" } EOF

curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json' \ -X PUT http://localhost/vault/users/1234567890 \ -d @- <<EOF { "firstName": "Joe", "lastName": "Doe", "email": "joe.doe@myorg.org" } EOF
curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json' \ -X POST http://localhost/vault/users/1234567890 \ -d @- <<EOF { "email": "joe@myorg.org" } EOF

curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'Accept: application/json' \ -X POST http://localhost/vault/users/1234567890 \ -d @- <<EOF [ [ "set_property", "firstName", "John" ], [ "remove_property", "lastName", "email" ] ] EOF
